caption: Naur's title is struck out: *Programming* becomes **Specs**.
Title card: *Specs as Theory Building*, the extended cut.
"What does a software team *actually* produce?" The team's printouts pile up. *The product?*
Naur's 1985 answer: **not the code.** The stack is crossed out and sparks rise over the team.
Peter Naur: editor of the **ALGOL 60** report, the **N in BNF**, **Turing Award** 2005.
The essay's own sections, read slowly. The chapters of this cut follow them.
The **production view**: programming produces a program and some other texts.
The **theory building view**: programmers form a theory; the texts are *secondary*.
Programming **matches** part of a real-world activity to symbol manipulation.
The world changes, so programming includes **modification** to keep the match.
Case 1: group B gets the compiler with full documentation, annotated code and **advice**.
B's proposals are patches that would destroy the design; group A **spots them instantly**.
Ten years on, without A: the structure is still visible but **made ineffective** by amorphous additions.
Case 2: the veterans fix faults from **what they know** and the annotated code.
Teams with full manuals get stuck; a veteran **clears it up easily**.
Gilbert Ryle: intelligent behaviour means **doing things well** and **catching your own lapses**.
Not rule-following: rules for applying the rules would **regress forever**.
Having a **theory** goes further: explain, answer questions, argue.
Newton's theory means seeing it in **pendulums and planets**, and recognizing **similar cases**.
Similarity can't be put into rules, so **a theory can't be fully written down**.
What the theory makes possible, 1: **map** each part to the world, including which parts matter.
2 **justify** and 3 **adapt**: meet a change by seeing how it resembles what's there.
Cheap to edit, so cheap to change? Naur: **false**. Text was never the main cost.
Renovating can cost more than rebuilding, and **flexibility costs now** for needs that may never come.
Many ways, all correct: some **extend the theory**, others are **patches**, and only a theory-holder can tell.
Simplicity and good structure make sense only against the programs that **could have been written**.
A program is **alive** while a team holding its theory controls its changes.
The team dissolves: the program **dies**, keeps running, and requests go unanswered.
Rebuilding the theory from code and documents alone: **strictly impossible**.
A theory is passed on like music: by **working closely** with people who have it.
A method is work rules, but a theory has **no inherent parts or order**.
**No right method**; methods help as education.
Not replaceable parts: **responsible, permanent developers**, with the standing of engineers and lawyers.
Agents make text nearly free. The cost **moves to specifying**.
An agent in a codebase is attempting **revival**: its picture differs from the original.
The spec is the handoff. The agent **gets the spec**; **you keep the theory**.
In a regulated enterprise the theory is scattered. **Requirements gathering is theory building.**
Starting each spec from scratch, every team rediscovers the **same rules, quirks and owners**.
The loop: discover, verify, specify, build, learn, then **write back governed facts**.
A governed fact: **source, owner, date, verified or assumed**. Decisions keep their reasons.
The next loop **starts from those facts**: adjacent work inherits them; unrelated work reuses shared rules, platforms and people.
Fewer unknowns, faster loops, and when a rule changes, **every spec that relied on it** lights up.
With Naur, not around him: facts are what the theory is built on, and its **holders stay in the loop**.
**Five habits** for PMs writing specs.
Code is the output. The spec is the handoff. **Governed facts are the memory. The theory is the product.**
